listeningParts.title: Booking a steam railway trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a heritage steam railway to book a day trip for her family.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Good morning, Moorvale Steam Railway, booking office. Gemma speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hi. I'm hoping to book a trip on one of your steam trains for my family. We're staying in the area for a couple of weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Lovely. Are you thinking of our standard return journey, or one of our special events?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: The standard service runs from Moorvale station up the valley to Highcross, at the top of the line, and then back again. The round trip takes around three hours, including a stop of forty minutes at Highcross, where there's a small museum about the history of the line. On certain days we also run special trains, like the Fish and Chip Express in the evening, or the Driver Experience, where you spend an hour on the footplate with the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The standard one sounds right. We've got three children, and I think an evening trip would be too late for the youngest.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: How old are the children?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Twelve, nine and four.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Children under five travel free, so you'd only pay for two of them. Which day were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Friday the fourteenth, if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm sorry, Friday is fully booked, because there's a large school group travelling that day. But I've got plenty of space on Saturday the fifteenth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday is fine. We're flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: There are three departures from Moorvale on Saturdays: ten fifteen, twelve thirty and half past two. The ten fifteen is pulled by our oldest locomotive, which was built in 1912, so it's very popular with enthusiasts.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My husband would love that. We'll take the ten fifteen.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Good choice. Now, for two adults and two children, the best option is our family ticket, which is fifty-eight pounds. If you bought the tickets separately, it would come to sixty-four, so you save a little.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great. Can we choose where we sit?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: You can. Most of the train is made up of carriages from the 1950s, but we also have an observation carriage at the back, with large windows at the end, so you can watch the track disappearing behind you. It's an extra three pounds per person, but children usually love it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Let's do that, then. And is there any food on board?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: There's a buffet car serving hot drinks, sandwiches and cakes. Or you're welcome to bring your own picnic. There are picnic tables at Highcross, beside the river, and it's a lovely spot if the weather's good.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. We'll probably bring our own.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Could I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's Rachel Hollingworth. That's H-O-L-L-I-N-G-W-O-R-T-H.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: My mobile is 0412 556 803. It's an Australian number, I'm afraid.

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: That's no problem. We'll only use it if there's a change to the service. Occasionally, in very dry weather, we have to replace the steam engine with a diesel, because sparks from the chimney can start fires in the fields beside the line. If that happens, we'll send you a text and offer you a discount or a refund.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I hadn't thought of that. And how do we get our tickets?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: I'll email you a booking confirmation, and you collect the actual tickets from the booking office at Moorvale on the day. Please arrive at least twenty minutes before departure, as the queue can be quite long on Saturdays.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there parking at the station?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a car park right next to it. It costs four pounds for the day, and the machine only takes coins, so make sure you bring some change with you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Good to know. Oh, one more thing. My father is coming to stay next month, and he's mad about trains. Do you sell gift vouchers?

dialogue.speaker: Clerk
dialogue.text: We do. They're available in any amount from ten pounds, and they're valid for a year. You can buy them online or in our shop at the station.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A visit to an air museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to an aviation museum and explains its layout.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Northfield Air Museum. My name's Dave, and I'll be your guide for the first part of your visit. Before we set off, I'll give you a bit of background and explain how the museum is laid out, so that you can explore on your own later.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum is built on the site of a real airfield, which opened in 1938 as a training base for pilots. After the war it was used by a flying club for many years, and when the club moved to a larger airport in the 1990s, a group of local residents campaigned to persuade the council to turn the site into a museum rather than sell it for housing. Today we have over sixty aircraft, and more than half of the people who work here are still volunteers, many of them retired engineers and pilots, so if you have a question, please ask them. They love to talk.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, a few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere, but please don't use a flash in Hangar Two, because some of the fabric-covered aircraft there are very old, and strong light can damage the materials over time. You're welcome to touch any aircraft that has a green sticker next to it, but please don't climb on anything unless a member of staff is with you.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let me explain the layout. We're standing in the entrance hall, and the first building you come to is Hangar One. This tells the story of the early days of flight, from the first balloons in the eighteenth century to the aircraft of the First World War. One of the most popular exhibits here is a full-size copy of a balloon basket, which children can climb into. You'll also find a set of display cases about women in aviation, including pilots who set long-distance records in the 1930s.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Hangar Two is our largest building, and it covers the golden age of passenger air travel, from the 1950s onwards. The highlight is the front section of a jumbo jet, which you can walk through, from the cockpit to the first-class cabin. It gives you a good idea of how luxurious flying used to be, and how much the seats have changed. In the same hangar, there's a collection of airline uniforms and a whole wall of old posters advertising holidays abroad, which many of our older visitors find quite nostalgic.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you'd like to see how air traffic was managed, head to the original control tower, at the far end of the site. It's been restored to look exactly as it did in the 1960s, with the original radio equipment. On the top floor, there's a viewing gallery, and on clear days you can watch planes landing at the international airport about twenty kilometres away. There's also a flight simulator up there, which you can book for fifteen-minute sessions at the information desk. It's very realistic, and I'll warn you now: most first-time pilots crash.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, there's the outdoor airfield, where we keep the larger military and cargo aircraft that won't fit inside. On the first Sunday of each month, we start the engines of some of our historic planes, and occasionally one of them actually takes off, weather permitting. That's also where you'll find our picnic area and the children's playground, which is designed to look like a small airport.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: As for food, the café is next to the shop in the entrance hall. It's run by volunteers, and all the money it makes goes towards restoring aircraft. Our current project is a small passenger plane from the 1950s, which was found in very poor condition in a farmer's field. The restoration has already taken four years, and we hope to finish it next summer. You can watch the volunteers at work through a glass window in the workshop behind Hangar One.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, I think that's everything. We'll start in Hangar One, and this part of the tour will take about forty-five minutes. Please stay together, and follow me.

listeningParts.title: Can trains replace short flights?
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two transport studies students, Maya and Tom, discuss their report on high-speed rail with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hi, Maya, hi, Tom. Come and sit down. So you're about halfway through your report on high-speed rail and short-haul flights. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've done most of the reading, and we've started looking at some case studies of routes where a fast rail line has opened alongside an existing air route.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Remind me what your main question is.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Basically, whether high-speed trains can take passengers away from planes on journeys of up to about a thousand kilometres, and what factors make the difference.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And what have you found so far?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: The clearest finding is that journey time is the most important factor, but it's the total journey time that matters, not just the time spent on the train or in the air. With a flight, you have to get out to the airport, which is often a long way from the city centre, arrive early for security checks, and then travel into the city at the other end. Stations are usually right in the centre.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: So several studies suggest that if the train takes less than about three hours, most people choose the train. Once it's more than four or five hours, flying usually wins.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's consistent with what I've read. Which case studies are you using?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The first one is Japan. The original Shinkansen line between Tokyo and Osaka opened in 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics, and it's still one of the busiest high-speed lines in the world. What impressed me most wasn't the speed, though, it was the reliability. The average delay is measured in seconds rather than minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Our second case study is France. The first TGV line, between Paris and Lyon, opened in 1981, and air traffic between the two cities fell sharply afterwards. More recently, France has banned some domestic flights on routes where there's a train alternative of less than two and a half hours.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That ban got a lot of attention. Did you find out how much difference it actually made?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Not a huge amount, to be honest. Only a few routes were affected, partly because there are exceptions for passengers who are connecting to other flights. And many people on those routes had already switched to the train anyway. So critics say it was more symbolic than practical.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point to make. A policy can matter symbolically even if its direct effect is small. What about cost?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: That was the most surprising part for us. We expected trains to be cheaper, but on many routes in Europe, budget airlines charge less than the train, especially if you book early. Part of the reason is tax. In many countries there's no tax on aviation fuel, whereas rail companies have to pay for electricity and for access to the track.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the cost of building the lines?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It's enormous. High-speed lines need very gentle curves and slopes, so they often require long tunnels and bridges, and in crowded countries buying the land is extremely expensive. That's why some people argue the money would be better spent improving existing railways.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, I'd like you to think about the environmental argument a bit more critically. It's often assumed that trains are always the greener choice.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: We were going to say that electric trains produce far lower emissions per passenger than planes, especially where the electricity comes from renewable sources.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's true once the trains are running. But building a new line produces a great deal of emissions, from all the concrete and steel. So the overall benefit depends on how many passengers use the line over its lifetime. A line with very few passengers might take decades to make up for its construction emissions.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We hadn't really thought about that. We could add a section on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Please do. And for your presentation next month, I'd suggest a map comparing the networks in Japan and France. Visuals help a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.text: Okay. Should we collect any data of our own?

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: A short survey of students about how they travel home at the end of term would be a nice addition. Keep it to ten questions at most, or people won't finish it.

listeningParts.title: From the Grand Tour to the package holiday
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a tourism history course on how travel for pleasure developed in Europe.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. In this lecture, I want to look at one of the most important chapters in the history of travel: the Grand Tour, and how it eventually gave way to something we would recognise today as modern tourism.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For most of history, people travelled because they had to. Merchants travelled to trade, soldiers to fight, and pilgrims to visit holy places. The idea of travelling mainly for education and pleasure is much more recent. From around the middle of the seventeenth century until the early nineteenth century, it became fashionable for wealthy young men, particularly from Britain, to spend a long period travelling around continental Europe. This was known as the Grand Tour. The term was popularised by an English priest, Richard Lassels, in a guide to Italy published in 1670.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The typical Grand Tourist was a young man from an aristocratic family, often in his early twenties, who had just finished his studies at Oxford or Cambridge. He would usually be accompanied by a tutor, whose job was to supervise his education and, ideally, his behaviour. These tutors were sometimes jokingly called 'bear-leaders', because they were said to lead their wild young students around like performing bears. The tour could last anything from a few months to several years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The main purpose was education. Young men were expected to improve their knowledge of languages, especially French and Italian, to study art and architecture, and to learn the manners of polite society. The most important destination was Italy, and above all Rome, where travellers could see the remains of the classical world they had read about at school in Latin and Greek texts. Florence, Venice and Naples were also essential stops.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Getting there was far from easy. Travelling through France meant long days in horse-drawn carriages on poor roads. To reach Italy, many travellers crossed the Alps by the Mont Cenis pass. Carriages could not be driven over the pass, so they were taken apart and carried by mules, while the travellers themselves were carried up and down the mountain in chairs by local porters. Many wrote home describing how terrified they had been.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Grand Tourists were also enthusiastic collectors. They brought home paintings, sculptures, books and antiquities, many of which can still be seen in the great country houses of Britain. Views of Venice by the painter Canaletto were especially popular, and in Rome many visitors had their portraits painted by Pompeo Batoni, often posing in front of famous ancient ruins. The excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii, which began in the 1730s and 1740s, added a new attraction, as travellers could watch buried Roman towns being uncovered.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: During the eighteenth century, the Grand Tour gradually became less exclusive, and growing numbers of middle-class travellers and women took part. But it was badly interrupted by the French Revolution and the wars that followed, which made travel across much of Europe dangerous until 1815.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The real transformation came with the railways. In 1841, Thomas Cook, a Baptist preacher who campaigned against alcohol, organised a special train to take around five hundred people from Leicester to a temperance meeting in Loughborough. The ticket cost one shilling, and the price included food. This trip is often described as the beginning of the package tour, because one person arranged the transport, the meals and the activities for a whole group. Cook went on to organise tours to Scotland, and later to continental Europe and beyond.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At around the same time, new guidebooks began to appear, such as those published by John Murray in Britain and Karl Baedeker in Germany, which gave practical information about routes, prices and hotels. Together, the railways, the guidebooks and the organised tour made travel for pleasure possible for millions of ordinary people. Next week, we'll look at how cheap air travel in the twentieth century transformed tourism all over again.

readingPassages.title: Lighter than air: the first balloon flights
paragraphs: On 4 June 1783, a crowd gathered in the market square of Annonay, a small town in south-eastern France, to watch an unusual experiment. Two brothers, Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier, lit a fire beneath an enormous bag made of cloth lined with paper. As it filled with hot smoke, the bag swelled, strained against the ropes holding it down and, when released, rose high into the sky. It stayed in the air for around ten minutes and came down a couple of kilometres away. The age of human flight had begun, not with wings, but with a bag of hot air.

The Montgolfiers were not scientists by training. They came from a family of paper manufacturers, and their knowledge of paper and fabric was essential to their success. According to a popular story, Joseph got the idea while watching clothes drying over a fire billow upwards, although this may be a later invention. What is certain is that the brothers did not fully understand why their balloons rose. They believed that burning produced a special gas, sometimes called 'Montgolfier gas', and they burned damp straw and wool to create as much thick smoke as possible. In fact, the explanation is simpler: hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it, and so it rises.

News of the Annonay experiment reached Paris quickly, and it inspired a rival. The physicist Jacques Charles knew that hydrogen, a gas that had been identified by the English scientist Henry Cavendish in 1766, was far lighter than air. Working with two brothers, Anne-Jean and Nicolas-Louis Robert, he built a small balloon of silk coated with rubber to keep the gas from escaping. On 27 August 1783 it was launched from the Champ de Mars in Paris. It flew for about forty-five minutes before coming down near the village of Gonesse, where frightened villagers, who had never seen anything like it, attacked it with pitchforks and knives.

The Montgolfiers, meanwhile, had been invited to demonstrate their invention at the royal palace of Versailles. On 19 September 1783, in front of King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette, they sent up a balloon carrying a basket containing a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Nobody knew whether living creatures could survive in the upper air, and the animals served as the first test passengers. The flight lasted around eight minutes, and the balloon landed safely about three kilometres away. All three animals survived, which encouraged the brothers to attempt a flight with people on board.

That flight took place on 21 November 1783, from the gardens of the Château de la Muette, on the western edge of Paris. The passengers were Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier, a young science teacher, and the Marquis d'Arlandes, an army officer. It is often said that the king had suggested sending condemned prisoners instead, since the risks were unknown, but that Pilâtre de Rozier objected that such an honour should not go to criminals. The two men stayed aloft for about twenty-five minutes and travelled roughly nine kilometres across the city. They had to keep feeding the fire with straw, and d'Arlandes later described using wet sponges to put out small fires that broke out in the fabric.

Only ten days later, on 1 December, Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert made the first manned flight in a hydrogen balloon, rising from the Tuileries Garden in front of an enormous crowd. They flew for around two hours and landed more than thirty kilometres away. Charles then went up again alone and climbed to around three thousand metres, where he suffered from intense cold and pain in his ears. He never flew again. His balloon, however, included features such as a valve for releasing gas, bags of sand used as ballast and a basket hanging from a net, and this design remained the basic pattern for gas balloons for more than a century.

The flights caused a sensation. Balloons appeared on fans, plates, clocks and furniture, and huge crowds gathered wherever a launch was announced. The American statesman Benjamin Franklin, who was living in Paris at the time, watched the early flights with great interest. When a sceptical observer asked him what use a balloon could possibly be, Franklin is said to have replied, 'What is the use of a newborn baby?' Practical uses did soon appear: scientists took instruments into the air to study the atmosphere, and in 1794 the French army used a balloon for observation at the Battle of Fleurus.

Ballooning was also dangerous. In January 1785, Jean-Pierre Blanchard and the American doctor John Jeffries became the first people to cross the English Channel by air, though they had to throw almost everything overboard, including some of their clothing, to stay up. Later that year, Pilâtre de Rozier tried to cross in the opposite direction in a balloon that combined hydrogen and hot air. It came down soon after take-off, and he and his companion became the first known victims of an air crash. Hot-air ballooning then declined for many years, until engineers developed modern balloons heated by propane burners around 1960, creating the popular sport we know today.

readingPassages.title: The railway that changed the world
paragraphs: On 15 September 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened to the public. It was not the world's first railway: wagons had run on wooden or iron rails for centuries, and the Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened in 1825, had already used steam locomotives to haul coal. But the Liverpool and Manchester was something new. It was the first railway to link two major cities, the first to rely on steam locomotives for all its regular services, and the first to run passenger trains according to a timetable. In many ways, it was the model for every main-line railway that followed.

The railway was built to solve a business problem. In the early nineteenth century, Manchester was the centre of the world's cotton industry, but the raw cotton its mills needed arrived by ship at the port of Liverpool, around fifty kilometres away. Goods travelled between the two cities by canal and river, which was slow and, according to the merchants, unreasonably expensive, since the canal companies faced little competition and could set their own charges. In winter, the canals sometimes froze, and in dry summers the water could run low. A group of Liverpool merchants concluded that a railway would be faster, cheaper and more reliable.

Not everyone agreed. The canal owners, naturally, saw the railway as a threat to their profits, and powerful landowners objected to a line crossing their estates. Opponents spread alarming claims that the smoke would kill birds, that sparks would set fire to crops and that cows would stop giving milk. The first attempt to obtain permission from Parliament, in 1825, failed after the engineer George Stephenson was questioned by lawyers for the opponents and was unable to defend serious errors in the survey of the route. A second application, based on a new route that avoided some of the most difficult estates, was approved in 1826.

Building the line was a major engineering achievement. The most famous obstacle was Chat Moss, a large area of bog so soft that a person could barely walk across it. Experts had declared that no railway could be built there. Stephenson's solution was to lay the track on hurdles of heather and brushwood, so that it effectively floated on the surface, and huge quantities of material disappeared into the bog before the line was stable. Elsewhere, workers cut a deep passage through solid rock at Olive Mount, dug a tunnel beneath Liverpool to reach the docks and built a viaduct of nine arches across the Sankey valley, where, ironically, the railway crossed over a canal.

Even as construction continued, the company's directors had not decided how the trains would be pulled. Some favoured horses, which were familiar and reliable. Others proposed stationary steam engines placed along the route, which would haul trains with long cables. To settle the question, the directors organised a public competition at Rainhill in October 1829, offering a prize of five hundred pounds for the best locomotive. Several machines took part, and one, called Novelty, was a favourite with the crowds because of its speed, but it broke down repeatedly. The winner was Rocket, built by George Stephenson and his son Robert, the only locomotive to complete the trials. Its design, which included a boiler with many small tubes to heat the water more efficiently, influenced locomotives for decades.

The opening day was meant to be a triumph, and the Prime Minister, the Duke of Wellington, travelled on the first train. But it was overshadowed by tragedy. During a stop to take on water, several passengers stepped down onto the line, among them William Huskisson, a Member of Parliament for Liverpool and a strong supporter of the railway. As he crossed the track to speak to the Duke, he was struck by Rocket, which was approaching on the other line. His leg was badly crushed, and he died that evening. His death was reported across the country and made him one of the first widely publicised victims of a railway accident.

Despite this sad beginning, the railway was a remarkable success. Its promoters had expected freight, especially cotton, to provide most of its business, but the number of people wanting to travel far exceeded their predictions. A journey that had taken several hours by stagecoach could now be completed in under two. Investors and engineers came from across Britain and abroad to study the line, and within a few years railways were being planned between all the major cities of Britain. By the 1840s, the country was in the grip of a 'railway mania', with hundreds of new lines proposed.

The influence of the Liverpool and Manchester can still be felt today. Stephenson built it to a gauge, or distance between the rails, of four feet eight and a half inches, a measurement he had used on earlier colliery lines. Because so many early railways were built by Stephenson and his followers, this became known as standard gauge, and it is now used by the majority of the world's railways. Much of the original route is still in use, and the Manchester terminus at Liverpool Road, often described as the world's oldest surviving passenger station, is now part of a museum of science and industry.

readingPassages.title: Should we fly less?
paragraphs: Within a single lifetime, flying has changed from a luxury enjoyed by a wealthy few into a routine part of modern life. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, airlines carried more than four billion passengers a year, and the industry expected that number to keep rising. Yet over the same period, concern about the climate has grown, and aviation has become a symbol of the conflict between personal freedom and environmental responsibility. In Sweden, a new word, flygskam, or 'flight shame', spread around 2018, as some people began to feel uncomfortable about the emissions caused by their travel. The climate campaigner Greta Thunberg, who refuses to fly, made the issue internationally famous when she crossed the Atlantic by sailing boat in 2019.

How large is the problem? Aviation is responsible for roughly two and a half per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions. That may seem modest, but it is not the whole story. Aircraft also release nitrogen oxides and water vapour at high altitude, and under certain conditions they create contrails, the long white lines of ice crystals that can trap heat in the atmosphere. When these effects are included, scientists estimate that aviation's share of human-caused warming is considerably larger. Moreover, while other sectors such as electricity generation are steadily reducing their emissions, aviation is one of the hardest to clean up, so its share is likely to grow.

The emissions are also very unevenly distributed. Most of the world's population has never taken a flight, while a small minority flies many times a year. One widely cited estimate suggests that around one per cent of the world's people are responsible for roughly half of the emissions from passenger flights. For this reason, some campaigners have proposed a frequent-flyer levy, a tax that would be low or even zero for a person's first flight each year but would rise steeply with every additional journey. Supporters argue that this would protect the annual family holiday while discouraging the habits of the most frequent travellers.

The aviation industry, unsurprisingly, prefers technological solutions. The most promising in the short term is sustainable aviation fuel, which can be made from waste materials such as used cooking oil, animal fats and agricultural leftovers, and which can be mixed with ordinary jet fuel without changes to engines. Over their whole life cycle, such fuels can produce far lower emissions than fossil fuels. However, at present they make up only a tiny fraction of the fuel used by airlines, they cost considerably more, and the supply of suitable waste is limited.

Electric aircraft are another possibility, and several small prototypes have already flown. The difficulty is weight. Even the best modern batteries store many times less energy per kilogram than jet fuel, so a battery-powered airliner capable of crossing an ocean is not realistic with current technology. Electric planes are therefore likely to be used first for small aircraft on short routes, such as those connecting islands. Aircraft powered by hydrogen have also been proposed, but they would require new aircraft designs and new infrastructure at airports, and are unlikely to be common for many years.

In the meantime, many airlines invite passengers to offset their emissions by paying a little extra for projects elsewhere, such as planting trees or protecting forests. Offsetting has been heavily criticised. It is often difficult to check whether a project really removes the carbon it claims, or whether the forest would have been protected anyway, and trees that are planted may later be cut down or destroyed by fire. Critics argue that offsets allow people to feel that they have solved the problem without changing their behaviour.

For shorter journeys, the alternative of the train is increasingly attractive. High-speed rail already competes successfully with air travel on many routes in Europe and Asia, and France has gone as far as banning some domestic flights where a train journey of less than two and a half hours is available. In Europe, night trains, many of which were cut in the early twenty-first century because they were losing money, have been making a comeback, allowing passengers to cover long distances while they sleep and to arrive in a city centre in the morning.

In my view, campaigns that rely on making individuals feel guilty are unlikely to achieve much on their own. Most people will continue to fly if flying remains cheap and convenient, and it is unfair to place the burden on the occasional traveller visiting family abroad. Greater responsibility, I believe, should fall on those who fly most often, which is why a frequent-flyer levy seems to me a fair idea. Nor should we forget that flying brings real benefits: it connects families separated by migration, and tourism by air supports jobs in many poorer countries. The aim should not be to end flying, but to make sure that its true environmental cost is reflected in its price.
